# Using a real AWS S3 bucket instead of R2

This repo's default artifact store is Cloudflare R2 (`terraform/artifacts/`), chosen
because R2 charges nothing for egress and pulling a multi-gigabyte image down a few
times a month is otherwise the dominant cost. See the [Publishing](publishing.md)
section of the README for that path.

`scripts/publish-image.sh` and `scripts/fetch-image.sh` talk to the bucket through the
plain `aws` CLI, and only pass a custom `--endpoint-url` when `AWS_ENDPOINT_URL` is set —
so real AWS S3 works with the same two scripts and zero code changes. This guide walks
through setting that up, for when a Cloudflare account isn't an option, or you have
compliance or cost-allocation reasons to keep everything inside AWS.

**Read [Cost](#cost-what-r2-was-avoiding) before you provision anything.** The R2 choice
elsewhere in this repo was not arbitrary, and S3 egress is the reason.

## Prerequisites

- An AWS account, and credentials with permission to create an S3 bucket and an IAM
  user (`AdministratorAccess`, or an equivalent scoped policy, for the one-time
  `terraform apply`).
- The [`aws` CLI](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/userguide/getting-started-install.html)
  installed and configured (`aws configure`) with those credentials — this is separate
  from the credentials the *bucket* will use, which Terraform creates fresh below.
- Terraform 1.6+, already a repo requirement (see the main [README](../README.md#requirements)).

## 1. Create the module

There's no `terraform/artifacts-s3/` in this repo — the R2 module is the maintained
default — so this is copy-pasted into place rather than already sitting there. Create
the directory and the three files below:

```bash
mkdir -p terraform/artifacts-s3
```

**`terraform/artifacts-s3/main.tf`**

```hcl
terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.6.0"
  required_providers {
    aws = {
      source  = "hashicorp/aws"
      version = "~> 5.0"
    }
  }
}

provider "aws" {
  region = var.aws_region
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket" "artifacts" {
  bucket = var.bucket_name
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket_versioning" "artifacts" {
  bucket = aws_s3_bucket.artifacts.id
  versioning_configuration {
    status = "Enabled"
  }
}

# Disables ACLs entirely in favour of IAM/bucket policies, which is the modern
# default AWS itself recommends for any new bucket.
resource "aws_s3_bucket_ownership_controls" "artifacts" {
  bucket = aws_s3_bucket.artifacts.id
  rule {
    object_ownership = "BucketOwnerEnforced"
  }
}

# These images are pulled with credentials, never served publicly, so every
# public-access path is blocked at the bucket level -- not just left unused.
resource "aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block" "artifacts" {
  bucket                  = aws_s3_bucket.artifacts.id
  block_public_acls       = true
  block_public_policy     = true
  ignore_public_acls      = true
  restrict_public_buckets = true
}

# Only cleans up abandoned multipart uploads. Build retention (keeping the
# newest N images) is handled by scripts/publish-image.sh itself -- a bucket
# lifecycle rule that also expired objects would be a second, uncoordinated
# place deciding what to delete, and the two would eventually disagree.
resource "aws_s3_bucket_lifecycle_configuration" "artifacts" {
  bucket = aws_s3_bucket.artifacts.id
  rule {
    id     = "abort-incomplete-multipart-uploads"
    status = "Enabled"
    abort_incomplete_multipart_upload {
      days_after_initiation = 7
    }
  }
}

resource "aws_iam_user" "publisher" {
  name = "${var.bucket_name}-publisher"
}

resource "aws_iam_access_key" "publisher" {
  user = aws_iam_user.publisher.name
}

# Scoped to exactly this bucket -- not AmazonS3FullAccess -- so a leaked key
# cannot touch anything else in the account.
resource "aws_iam_user_policy" "publisher" {
  name = "${var.bucket_name}-rw"
  user = aws_iam_user.publisher.name
  policy = jsonencode({
    Version = "2012-10-17"
    Statement = [
      {
        Sid      = "ListBucket"
        Effect   = "Allow"
        Action   = ["s3:ListBucket"]
        Resource = [aws_s3_bucket.artifacts.arn]
      },
      {
        Sid      = "ReadWriteObjects"
        Effect   = "Allow"
        Action   = ["s3:GetObject", "s3:PutObject", "s3:DeleteObject"]
        Resource = ["${aws_s3_bucket.artifacts.arn}/*"]
      }
    ]
  })
}
```

**`terraform/artifacts-s3/variables.tf`**

```hcl
variable "bucket_name" {
  type        = string
  default     = "workstation-artifacts"
  description = "Must be globally unique across ALL of AWS, not just this account -- unlike R2's bucket namespace, which is scoped to your account. The default name will very likely already be taken; pick something specific to you."
}

variable "aws_region" {
  type        = string
  default     = "us-east-1"
  description = "Where the bucket physically lives. Pick the region closest to wherever you build and fetch images, since that distance is what the egress cost and latency below are actually paying for."
}
```

**`terraform/artifacts-s3/outputs.tf`**

```hcl
output "bucket_name" {
  value = aws_s3_bucket.artifacts.id
}

output "aws_region" {
  value = var.aws_region
}

output "access_key_id" {
  value = aws_iam_access_key.publisher.id
}

output "secret_access_key" {
  value     = aws_iam_access_key.publisher.secret
  sensitive = true
}
```

## 2. Apply it

```bash
cd terraform/artifacts-s3
terraform init
terraform apply
```

Terraform will print a plan naming the bucket, the IAM user, and the access key it is
about to create. Review the bucket name in particular — a global collision fails the
apply with `BucketAlreadyExists`, not a warning, so if the default is taken pass
`-var bucket_name=your-own-unique-name`.

## 3. Set your environment

```bash
export WORKSTATION_BUCKET=$(terraform output -raw bucket_name)
export AWS_DEFAULT_REGION=$(terraform output -raw aws_region)
export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=$(terraform output -raw access_key_id)
export AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=$(terraform output -raw secret_access_key)
```

**Do not set `AWS_ENDPOINT_URL`.** If you have followed the R2 guide before on the same
machine, unset it:

```bash
unset AWS_ENDPOINT_URL
```

This is the one step that is easy to get wrong by copying the R2 instructions verbatim.
`scripts/publish-image.sh` and `scripts/fetch-image.sh` only add `--endpoint-url` to the
`aws` CLI when that variable is set — it exists specifically to redirect the CLI at R2's
non-AWS endpoint. Leaving an old R2 endpoint set here does not fail loudly: `aws` will
try to talk to the wrong host and the error will look like a network or auth problem,
not "you forgot to unset a variable."

Also do not set `AWS_DEFAULT_REGION=auto` — that value is an R2-ism (R2 has no regions
to choose between) and is not valid for a real AWS S3 request signature.

`cd` back to the repo root before continuing; the scripts expect to run from there.

## 4. Try it

```bash
make publish VERSION=$(make version)   # after `make image` has produced a build
make fetch                             # on this or another machine
```

`fetch-image.sh` verifies SHA256SUMS before treating anything as usable, so a
successful `make fetch` is a genuine end-to-end confirmation: the bucket accepted the
upload, the channel pointer moved, and the checksum on the way back down matches.

## 5. Wire it into CI (optional)

`.github/workflows/build.yml` reads the publish step's credentials from GitHub secrets
named `R2_ENDPOINT_URL`, `R2_ACCESS_KEY_ID` and `R2_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` — names left over
from the default R2 path. Only the *values* matter to the scripts, so the simplest way
to point CI at a real S3 bucket without editing the workflow is:

| GitHub secret | Value |
|---|---|
| `WORKSTATION_BUCKET` | the bucket name from step 3 |
| `R2_ACCESS_KEY_ID` | the IAM access key ID from step 3 |
| `R2_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` | the IAM secret access key from step 3 |
| `R2_ENDPOINT_URL` | **do not create this secret at all** |

An unset GitHub secret resolves to an empty string, `AWS_ENDPOINT_URL` ends up empty,
and `aws_s3()` in both scripts takes the plain-`aws` branch — exactly the behaviour you
want. If a `R2_ENDPOINT_URL` secret already exists from a previous R2 setup, delete it
rather than leaving it, for the same reason as step 3.

Also set `AWS_DEFAULT_REGION` to your bucket's region in the workflow's `env:` block (it
is currently hardcoded to R2's `auto`), or the scheduled/tag-triggered publish step will
sign requests for the wrong region and fail.

## Security notes

- **The Terraform state file contains the IAM secret access key in plaintext**, because
  `terraform output` has to be able to print it. `*.tfstate` is already gitignored — never
  commit it regardless — and treat wherever the state lives (local disk, or a remote
  backend if you configure one) as holding a live credential.
- **Rotate the access key periodically.** `terraform apply` after changing nothing will
  not rotate it for you; that needs `terraform taint aws_iam_access_key.publisher` (or
  the newer `terraform apply -replace=aws_iam_access_key.publisher`) followed by
  `apply`, then updating wherever you exported the old values.
- The IAM policy is scoped to this one bucket. If you ever see `AccessDenied` on an
  otherwise-correct bucket name, check that the IAM user's policy still matches the
  bucket ARN — a bucket recreated under a new name needs the policy updated too, which
  `terraform apply` handles automatically as long as you didn't hand-edit the bucket
  outside Terraform.

## Cost: what R2 was avoiding

This is the tradeoff the rest of the repo's Terraform sidesteps, made explicit so it's a
choice rather than a surprise on next month's bill:

- **Storage**: ~$0.023/GB-month for S3 Standard. A handful of image builds is a
  rounding error here.
- **Requests**: PUT/GET pricing is negligible at this volume (one publish, occasional
  fetches).
- **Egress — the one that matters**: ~$0.09/GB to transfer data *out* of S3 to the
  internet. A compressed workstation image is multiple GB. Pull it down to flash a new
  laptop, then again next month for the next one, and this line item adds up in a way
  storage and requests do not. R2 charges nothing for this.

If you're setting this up because you're already paying for AWS and want everything in
one place, or because of a compliance requirement that specifically calls for AWS, that
tradeoff is probably fine. If the only reason is "I don't have a Cloudflare account,"
creating one costs nothing and the [R2 path](publishing.md) avoids the egress
line entirely.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Likely cause |
|---|---|
| `BucketAlreadyExists` on `terraform apply` | S3 bucket names are global. Pick a more specific `bucket_name`. |
| `make fetch` / `make publish` hang or time out talking to a host that isn't AWS | `AWS_ENDPOINT_URL` is still set from a previous R2 setup. `unset` it. |
| `SignatureDoesNotMatch` or requests failing against the right bucket | `AWS_DEFAULT_REGION` doesn't match the bucket's actual region, or is left as R2's `auto`. |
| `AccessDenied` | Credentials are for the wrong IAM user, the policy doesn't cover the bucket ARN, or the bucket was renamed outside Terraform without re-applying. |
| CI publish step fails after switching from R2 | A stale `R2_ENDPOINT_URL` secret still exists — delete it, don't just leave it blank in the workflow file. |
